exercises.title: Least-squares line from normal equations
exercises.description: Determine the least-squares line $y = c_0 + c_1t$ through $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,4)$ using the normal equations.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$A^TAx = A^Tb$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $b = (1,2,4)^T$.

Step 2: Normal equations
$A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$, $A^Tb = \begin{pmatrix}7\\10\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Solving
$\det = 15 - 9 = 6$. $x = \tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}5&-3\\-3&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}7\\10\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}5\\9\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.8333\\1.5\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Line: $y = 0.833 + 1.5t$. The residual is orthogonal to both columns of $A$.

exercises.title: Setting up A and b
exercises.description: Set up the matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ for the measurements $(1,2), (2,3), (3,5), (4,4)$ and the model $y = c_0 + c_1t$. How many equations and unknowns are there?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Each measurement $(t_i, y_i)$ yields a row $(1, t_i)\,x = y_i$.

Step 2: System
$A = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$, $x = \begin{pmatrix}c_0\\c_1\end{pmatrix}$, $b = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Count
$m = 4$ equations, $n = 2$ unknowns: overdetermined. No line passes through all the points.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Measurements = rows, parameters = columns.

exercises.title: Computing the residual
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, $b = (1,2,2,4)^T$ and $x = (0.9, 0.9)^T$: compute $r = b - Ax$, $\|r\|_2^2$ and check $A^Tr = 0$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
First $Ax$, then subtract.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The residual of the least-squares solution is perpendicular to $\mathrm{range}(A)$ – that is the check.

exercises.title: Checking orthogonality
exercises.description: Is $Q = \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.8\\-0.8&0.6\end{pmatrix}$ orthogonal? Compute $\|Qx\|_2$ for $x = (3,4)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Check $Q^TQ = I$, then compute $Qx$.

Step 3: Norm preservation
$Qx = (0.6\cdot3 + 0.8\cdot4,\ -0.8\cdot3 + 0.6\cdot4) = (5, 0)^T$, $\|Qx\|_2 = 5 = \|x\|_2$ ✓.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The columns (and rows) of $Q$ are orthonormal; $Q$ only rotates or reflects.

exercises.title: Givens rotation
exercises.description: Determine $c$ and $s$ such that $G\binom{3}{4} = \binom{r}{0}$ with $G = \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, $c = a/r$, $s = b/r$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The minus sign is in the lower left: $G = \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}$ zeroes the second component.

exercises.title: Gram–Schmidt in ℝ²
exercises.description: Orthonormalise $a_1 = (3,4)^T$, $a_2 = (1,2)^T$ with Gram–Schmidt and state $R$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$q_1 = a_1/\|a_1\|$; then remove from $a_2$ the component in direction $q_1$.

Step 4: Result
$R = \begin{pmatrix}5&2.2\\0&0.4\end{pmatrix}$ – the same as in the Givens computation in the lesson. $q_1^Tq_2 = -0.48 + 0.48 = 0$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
QR is unique up to signs (completely unique if one requires $r_{ii} > 0$).

exercises.title: Solution from a given QR
exercises.description: Let $A = QR$ with $R = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $Q^Tb = (5, 3)^T$ (square case). Determine $x$ from $Ax = b$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$Ax = b \iff QRx = b \iff Rx = Q^Tb$.

Step 2: Backward
$3x_2 = 3 \Rightarrow x_2 = 1$. $2x_1 + x_2 = 5 \Rightarrow x_1 = 2$.

Step 3: Result
$x = (2, 1)^T$. Cost: only a matrix–vector product with $Q^T$ and back substitution.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
$Q^{-1} = Q^T$ – the inverse of $Q$ is free.

exercises.title: Number of equations and unknowns
exercises.description: For seven measurements $(t_i, y_i)$ a polynomial $y = c_0 + c_1t + c_2t^2$ is to be fitted. What size is $A$, and what size is $A^TA$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Rows = measurements, columns = parameters.

Step 2: Sizes
$A \in \mathbb R^{7\times3}$ with rows $(1, t_i, t_i^2)$. $A^TA \in \mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $A^Tb \in \mathbb R^3$.

Step 3: Consequence
The normal equations are a small $3\times3$ system no matter how many measurements there are – that is their advantage for $m \gg n$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
$m \times n$ with $m > n$; $A^TA$ is $n \times n$. The model is linear in the parameters $c_i$ although it is quadratic in $t$.

exercises.title: Least-squares parabola
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Matrix $A$ with columns $1, t, t^2$, then $A^TAx = A^Tb$.

Step 2: Normal equations
$\sum 1 = 4$, $\sum t = 2$, $\sum t^2 = 6$, $\sum t^3 = 8$, $\sum t^4 = 18$; $\sum y = 6$, $\sum ty = 7$, $\sum t^2y = 15$. $\begin{pmatrix}4&2&6\\2&6&8\\6&8&18\end{pmatrix}x = \begin{pmatrix}6\\7\\15\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Solution
Elimination gives $x = (0.6,\ 0.3,\ 0.5)^T$, so $y = 0.6 + 0.3t + 0.5t^2$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Model linear in the coefficients ⇒ linear least-squares problem, also for higher polynomial degrees. But beware: $\mathrm{cond}$ grows quickly with the degree.

exercises.title: Gram–Schmidt for a 3×2 matrix
exercises.description: Compute the QR decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with Gram–Schmidt and use it to solve the least-squares problem for $b = (1,2,3)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
First $q_1, q_2, R$, then $R_1x = Q^Tb$.

Step 4: Right-hand side
$c_1 = q_1^Tb = 2.1213$, $c_2 = q_2^Tb = 2.0412$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Check with normal equations: $A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $A^Tb = (3,4)$ gives the same $x = (\frac23,\frac53)$ ✓.

exercises.title: Householder vector in ℝ³
exercises.description: For $x = (2,1,2)^T$ determine the Householder vector $v$, the matrix $H$ and verify $Hx = (-3,0,0)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$v = x + \mathrm{sign}(x_1)\|x\|e_1$, $H = I - \frac{2vv^T}{v^Tv}$.

Step 3: H
$H = I - \tfrac{1}{15}vv^T = \tfrac1{15}\begin{pmatrix}-10&-5&-10\\-5&14&-2\\-10&-2&11\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For $x_1 > 0$ choose $+\|x\|$ in $v$ (target $-\|x\|e_1$) to avoid cancellation in $v_1$. $H$ is symmetric and orthogonal.

exercises.title: Givens QR of a 2×2 matrix
exercises.description: Compute the QR decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$ with a Givens rotation and solve $Ax = (4, 6)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
One rotation zeroes the entry $a_{21} = 4$.

Step 2: Rotation
$(a,b) = (3,4)$: $r = 5$, $c = 0.6$, $s = 0.8$, $G = \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.8\\-0.8&0.6\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: R
$R = GA$: column 1 $= (5, 0)$; column 2: $(0.6\cdot1 + 0.8\cdot2,\ -0.8\cdot1 + 0.6\cdot2) = (2.2, 0.4)$. $R = \begin{pmatrix}5&2.2\\0&0.4\end{pmatrix}$, $Q = G^T$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Check: $A(1,1)^T = (4, 6)^T$ ✓. $G$ is applied to the right-hand side as well – carry the rotations along!

exercises.title: Linearising an exponential model
exercises.description: Fit $y = ae^{bt}$ to $(0,2), (1,6), (2,17)$ by fitting $\ln y$ linearly in $t$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\ln y = \ln a + bt$ is a linear least-squares problem in $(\ln a, b)$.

Step 4: Model
$a = e^{0.7027} = 2.019$, $y \approx 2.019\,e^{1.07t}$ (growth factor per unit time $e^{1.07} = 2.915$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
This minimises errors in $\ln y$ – large $y$ values are weighted relatively less than in a direct fit.

exercises.title: Conditioning: normal equations vs. QR
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0.01&0\\0&0.01\end{pmatrix}$ we have $A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}1.0001&1\\1&1.0001\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\mathrm{cond}_2(A^TA)$ and $\mathrm{cond}_2(A)$ and explain why QR is preferable.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$A^TA$ is symmetric: eigenvalues directly.

Step 2: Eigenvalues
$\lambda_{1,2} = 1.0001 \pm 1$: $\lambda_1 = 2.0001$, $\lambda_2 = 0.0001$.

Step 3: Condition numbers
$\mathrm{cond}_2(A^TA) = 2.0001/0.0001 = 20001$. $\mathrm{cond}_2(A) = \sqrt{20001} = 141.4$ (singular values $\sqrt{\lambda}$).

Step 4: Consequence
Normal equations solve a system with condition $2\cdot10^4$ instead of $141$: they lose $\approx 4.3$ instead of $\approx 2.2$ digits. QR works on $R$ with $\mathrm{cond}(R) = \mathrm{cond}(A) = 141$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Squared condition = twice the digit loss. For $\mathrm{cond}(A) \approx 10^8$, $A^TA$ is numerically singular.

exercises.title: Projection onto range(A)
exercises.description: Project $b = (1,2,3)^T$ onto the range of $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and verify the orthogonality of the remainder.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Projection: $p = Ax$ with $A^TAx = A^Tb$.

Step 2: Normal equations
$A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $A^Tb = (3, 5)^T$. $x = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix} = (\tfrac13, \tfrac73)^T$.

Step 3: Projection
$p = Ax = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac83,\ \tfrac73)^T$.

Step 4: Remainder
$r = b - p = (\tfrac23, -\tfrac23, \tfrac23)^T$. $r\cdot a_1 = \tfrac23 - \tfrac23 = 0$, $r\cdot a_2 = -\tfrac23 + \tfrac23 = 0$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
$b = p + r$ splits $b$ into a part in the range and one perpendicular to it (Pythagoras: $\|b\|^2 = \|p\|^2 + \|r\|^2$: $14 = 10\tfrac23 + \tfrac43\ \ ✓$).

exercises.title: Weighted least squares
exercises.description: The measurement $(2,2)$ is particularly reliable and gets weight $4$, the others $(0,1), (1,2), (3,4)$ get weight $1$. Minimise $\sum w_ir_i^2$ for $y = c_0 + c_1t$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Weighted normal equations $A^TWAx = A^TWb$ with $W = \mathrm{diag}(w_i)$.

Step 3: System
$\begin{pmatrix}7&12\\12&26\end{pmatrix}x = \begin{pmatrix}15\\30\end{pmatrix}$, $\det = 182 - 144 = 38$.

Step 4: Solution
$x = \tfrac1{38}\begin{pmatrix}26&-12\\-12&7\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}15\\30\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac1{38}\begin{pmatrix}30\\30\end{pmatrix} = (0.789, 0.789)^T$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The line $y = 0.789(1 + t)$ now passes closer to $(2, 2)$ ($2.37$ instead of $2.7$ for equally weighted data). Weights $= 1/\sigma_i^2$ for known measurement errors.

exercises.title: Normal equations via the gradient
exercises.description: Derive the normal equations by differentiating $\varphi(x) = \|Ax - b\|_2^2$ with respect to $x$ and show that it is a minimum.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Expand: $\varphi(x) = x^TA^TAx - 2b^TAx + b^Tb$.

Step 2: Gradient
$\nabla\varphi(x) = 2A^TAx - 2A^Tb$ (since $A^TA$ is symmetric).

Step 3: Necessary condition
$\nabla\varphi = 0 \iff A^TAx = A^Tb$.

Step 4: Sufficient
The Hessian $\nabla^2\varphi = 2A^TA$ is positive semidefinite ($z^TA^TAz = \|Az\|^2 \ge 0$), positive definite for full column rank. So a (global, unique) minimum.

Step 5: Alternative
Geometrically: $\varphi$ minimal $\iff r = b - Ax \perp \mathrm{range}(A) \iff A^Tr = 0$ – the same result without calculus.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Quadratic function with positive definite Hessian ⇒ exactly one minimum, found through a linear system.

exercises.title: Uniqueness for full column rank
exercises.description: Show: if $A \in \mathbb R^{m\times n}$ has full column rank, then $A^TA$ is positive definite (hence invertible) and the least-squares solution is unique. What happens when rank is lost?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Consider the quadratic form $z^TA^TAz = \|Az\|_2^2$.

Step 2: Definiteness
For $z \ne 0$ we have $Az \ne 0$ (full column rank = kernel $\{0\}$), so $z^TA^TAz = \|Az\|^2 > 0$. $A^TA$ is symmetric positive definite, hence invertible.

Step 3: Uniqueness
The normal equations then have exactly the solution $x = (A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$.

Step 4: Rank loss
If $\ker(A) \ne \{0\}$, then together with $x$ also $x + z$ ($z \in \ker(A)$) is a solution: infinitely many. One picks the one with minimal norm (pseudoinverse $x = A^+b$, via SVD).

Step 5: Example
Fitting a line with only a single measurement time $t = 2$ (repeated): columns $(1,1,1)$ and $(2,2,2)$ are linearly dependent – infinitely many lines fit equally well.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Full column rank ⇔ the parameters are uniquely determined by the data (identifiability).

exercises.title: Householder QR (3×2) in full
exercises.description: Compute the QR decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ with Householder reflections.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Two reflections: $H_1$ zeroes column 1 below the diagonal, $H_2$ zeroes column 2 below the diagonal.

Step 2: H₁
$x = (2,1,2)^T$: $v_1 = (5,1,2)^T$ (as above), $H_1x = (-3,0,0)^T$. Second column: $H_1(1,3,1)^T = \bigl(-\tfrac73,\ \tfrac73,\ -\tfrac13\bigr)^T$.

Step 3: After H₁
$H_1A = \begin{pmatrix}-3&-\tfrac73\\0&\tfrac73\\0&-\tfrac13\end{pmatrix}$. Now process the partial column $y = (\tfrac73, -\tfrac13)^T$: $\|y\|_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{49 + 1}{9}} = \tfrac{5\sqrt2}{3} = 2.357$.

Step 5: Result
$R = \begin{pmatrix}-3&-2.333\\0&-2.357\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Signs negative ($r_{ii} < 0$) – usual with Householder, multiplying by $-1$ enforces $r_{ii} > 0$. Check: $|r_{11}||r_{22}| = 7.07 = \sqrt{\det(A^TA)} = \sqrt{50}$ ✓ ($A^TA = \begin{pmatrix}9&7\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$, $\det = 50$).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
$R$ is invariant (up to signs) with respect to the computing method; $A^TA = R^TR$ serves as a check.

exercises.title: Proving residual ⊥ range(A)
exercises.description: Prove: $x^*$ solves $\min\|Ax - b\|_2$ if and only if $b - Ax^* \perp \mathrm{range}(A)$. Conclude the Pythagorean identity $\|b\|^2 = \|Ax^*\|^2 + \|r\|^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compare $\|Ax - b\|^2$ for arbitrary $x$ with $\|Ax^* - b\|^2$.

Step 2: Splitting
With $r = b - Ax^*$ and $d = x - x^*$: $b - Ax = r - Ad$. So $\|b - Ax\|^2 = \|r\|^2 - 2r^TAd + \|Ad\|^2$.

Step 3: Forward direction
If $A^Tr = 0$ the mixed term vanishes: $\|b - Ax\|^2 = \|r\|^2 + \|Ad\|^2 \ge \|r\|^2$. So $x^*$ is a minimum.

Step 4: Reverse direction
If $A^Tr \ne 0$, choose $d = tA^Tr$ with small $t > 0$: $-2t\|A^Tr\|^2 + t^2\|AA^Tr\|^2 < 0$ – then $\|b - Ax\| < \|r\|$, contradicting minimality.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Orthogonal projection is the best approximation – the geometric core of the method of least squares.

exercises.title: ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖ and its consequence
exercises.description: Prove $\|Qx\|_2 = \|x\|_2$ for orthogonal $Q$ and conclude that $\min\|Ax - b\|_2 = \min\|Rx - Q^Tb\|_2$ for $A = QR$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Use $\|y\|_2^2 = y^Ty$.

Step 2: Norm preservation
$\|Qx\|^2 = x^TQ^TQx = x^Tx = \|x\|^2$.

Step 3: Application
For $A = QR$ with square orthogonal $Q \in \mathbb R^{m\times m}$ and $R \in \mathbb R^{m\times n}$: $\|Ax - b\| = \|Q(Rx - Q^Tb)\| = \|Rx - Q^Tb\|$.

Step 4: Splitting up
With $R = \binom{R_1}{0}$, $Q^Tb = \binom{c_1}{c_2}$: $\|Rx - Q^Tb\|^2 = \|R_1x - c_1\|^2 + \|c_2\|^2$. The minimum ($R_1x = c_1$) leaves $\|c_2\|^2$.

Step 5: Consequence
Minimal residual $\|r\|_2 = \|c_2\|_2$ – without computing $x$. Example four points: $\|c_2\|^2 = \|b\|^2 - \|c_1\|^2 = 25 - (4.5^2 + 2.0125^2) = 25 - 24.3 = 0.7$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
An orthogonal transformation does not change the objective – that is why QR is stable (no squaring of the condition).

exercises.title: Classical vs. modified Gram–Schmidt
exercises.description: Consider $a_1 = (1,\varepsilon,0,0)^T$, $a_2 = (1,0,\varepsilon,0)^T$, $a_3 = (1,0,0,\varepsilon)^T$ with $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$ in double precision. Explain why classical Gram–Schmidt loses orthogonality (result $q_2^Tq_3 \approx 0.5$) but modified does not ($\approx 10^{-16}$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The columns are almost parallel; orthogonalising means subtracting almost equal vectors (cancellation).

Step 2: Step 1
$q_1 = a_1/\|a_1\|$, $\|a_1\|^2 = 1 + \varepsilon^2 = 1$ in double precision ($\varepsilon^2 = 10^{-16} < u$): $q_1 = a_1$.

Step 3: Steps 2 and 3
$a_2 - (q_1^Ta_2)q_1 = (0, -\varepsilon, \varepsilon, 0)$, likewise $v_3 = (0,-\varepsilon,0,\varepsilon)$ after subtracting $q_1$. Both remainders contain the information only at order $\varepsilon$ (cancellation!), but $q_2 = (0,-1,1,0)/\sqrt2$ is still clean.

Step 4: Classical
Classically all coefficients are formed with the original $a_3 = (1,0,0,\varepsilon)$: $q_2 = (0,-1,1,0)/\sqrt2$ has no overlap with $a_3$, so $q_2^Ta_3 = 0$ – nothing is subtracted against $q_2$. The remainder $v_3 = a_3 - q_1 = (0, -\varepsilon, 0, \varepsilon)$, however, has a component $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt2}$ along $q_2$. Result: $q_2^Tq_3 = \tfrac{\varepsilon/\sqrt2}{\varepsilon\sqrt2} = 0.5$ instead of $0$.

Step 5: Modified
Modified projects against the already cleaned remainder $v = a_3 - q_1$: $q_2^Tv = \tfrac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt2} \ne 0$ is subtracted. $q_2^Tq_3 = 1.1\cdot10^{-16}$ – orthogonal up to rounding.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Loss of orthogonality $\approx \mathrm{cond}(A)^2u$ (classical) or $\mathrm{cond}(A)u$ (modified). Householder: $O(u)$ independent of $\mathrm{cond}$.

exercises.title: Cost: Householder vs. normal equations
exercises.description: For $m = 1000$, $n = 10$ compare the cost of the normal equations ($mn^2 + \frac13n^3$) with that of Householder QR ($2mn^2 - \frac23n^3$) and explain when you choose QR anyway.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Plug in and form the ratio.

Step 2: Normal equations
$mn^2 = 1000\cdot100 = 10^5$, $\tfrac13n^3 = 333$: $\approx 1.003\cdot10^5$ flops (forming $A^TA$ dominates; symmetry is already exploited).

Step 3: Householder
$2mn^2 = 2\cdot10^5$, $\tfrac23n^3 = 667$: $\approx 1.993\cdot10^5$ flops.

Step 4: Ratio
$\tfrac{1.993}{1.003} \approx 2$: QR costs about twice as much.

Step 5: When QR?
Always when $\mathrm{cond}(A)$ could be large ($> 10^4$): normal equations lose twice as many digits. A factor of $2$ in computing time is cheaper than a wrong result. For very well-conditioned $A$ and large $m$ normal equations are acceptable.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Computing cost is rarely the main problem – stability is. QR is the standard method (e.g. MATLAB backslash).

exercises.title: Constrained least squares (idea)
exercises.description: Fit $y = c_0 + c_1t$ to $(0,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,4)$ but with the line passing through the point $(0,1)$ ($c_0 = 1$). Determine $c_1$ and compare the sum of squared residuals with the free fit ($0.7$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Inserting the constraint reduces the problem to one parameter.

Step 2: Reduced problem
$\min\sum(y_i - 1 - c_1t_i)^2$. With $\tilde y_i = y_i - 1 = (0, 1, 1, 3)$: $c_1 = \dfrac{\sum t_i\tilde y_i}{\sum t_i^2} = \dfrac{0 + 1 + 2 + 9}{0 + 1 + 4 + 9} = \dfrac{12}{14} = 0.857$.

Step 4: Comparison
$0.714$ versus $0.7$ for the free fit – only slightly worse because the free intercept $0.9$ is close to $1$.

Step 5: General idea
For $Cx = d$ with several constraints one uses Lagrange multipliers (KKT system) or the null-space method (QR of $C^T$).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Constraints never improve the minimum – it is a minimum over a smaller set.
